statements.text: Visible light is the small part of the spectrum our eyes can see, so visible images show Earth much as we would see it.
Weather satellites use visible channels to track clouds, fog, haze, dust, snow cover and volcanic ash.

conditions.label: Daytime only
conditions.text: Visible bands record reflected sunlight; NOAA lists ABI's red band as daytime only.

conditions.label: Blocked by cloud
conditions.text: Observations hidden by clouds and their shadows have to be thrown away.

uses.text: The Copernicus Land Monitoring Service maps vegetation seasons across Europe at 10 m from Sentinel-2.

statements.text: Plants reflect near-infrared light very strongly, so images that use it make vegetated land stand out.

conditions.label: Daytime only
conditions.text: Near infrared is reflected sunlight, like visible light.

conditions.label: Sees through haze
conditions.text: Near infrared can penetrate haze, which helps in smoky or hazy scenes.

uses.text: The US Department of Agriculture's Crop-CASMA tool uses MODIS reflectance at 250 m to compute a vegetation index for US crops.

statements.text: Newly burned land reflects strongly in shortwave infrared, which makes it valuable for mapping fire damage.
In a common shortwave infrared, near infrared and green combination, water looks black, plants bright green, newly burned land red, and snow and ice bright blue.
A shortwave infrared band at 3.9 µm is sensitive to the hottest part of a fire, so GOES often detects fires before they are spotted on the ground.

conditions.label: Less affected by smoke and dust
conditions.text: Shortwave infrared is less affected by scattering from fog, dust and smoke than visible light.

uses.text: Water absorbs shortwave infrared at 1,400, 1,900 and 2,400 nm, so it helps estimate how much water is in plants and soil.
The US Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity programme maps large fires from Landsat, and USGS measures burns with the Normalized Burn Ratio of near and shortwave infrared.

statements.text: Warm surfaces give off infrared radiation: energy absorbed by the ocean, for example, is re-emitted as infrared.
NOAA likens its infrared channels to night-vision goggles, because they see by day and by night.
Forecasters use cloud-top temperatures as predictors of rainfall intensity and flash flooding.

conditions.label: Works at night
conditions.text: The ground gives off thermal infrared, so it can be observed day and night.

conditions.label: Blocked by cloud
conditions.text: Infrared sensors cannot see through cloud, which typically limits sea surface temperature to about 20 percent of the ocean.

uses.text: NASA's FIRMS delivers MODIS and VIIRS fire detections worldwide within 3 hours of the satellite passing over.
NOAA CoastWatch makes operational sea surface temperature maps from VIIRS, ABI and AHI, among others.
NOAA Coral Reef Watch monitors heat stress that bleaches corals, worldwide at 5 km.

statements.text: GOES has three infrared bands, at 6.2, 6.9 and 7.3 µm, that track water vapour in the upper, middle and lower atmosphere.
The VIIRS Day/Night Band is a single wide band, sensitive to visible and near-infrared light, that records Earth's lights at night.
Its signal includes city lights, lightning, fishing fleet lights, gas flares, lava flows and even auroras.
Moonlight reflected off ice, snow and other bright surfaces shows up too.

conditions.label: Works at night
conditions.text: The Day/Night Band captures low-light images of Earth at night, down to quarter-moon light.

uses.text: NASA's Black Marble night lights are used to assess disruptions and recovery after disasters.

statements.text: SMAP measures the amount of water in the surface soil everywhere on Earth, every 2–3 days.

conditions.label: Works at night
conditions.text: SMAP measures the top 5 cm of soil through clouds and moderate vegetation, day and night.

conditions.label: Sees through cloud
conditions.text: Microwave sensors see through clouds, except heavy rain, but with coarse pixels of about 20 to 50 km.

uses.text: ECMWF feeds microwave measurements of humidity, cloud and rain into its weather forecasts; in 2019 they gave around 15 percent of the impact of all observations.
NOAA's ATMS sounder measures temperature and moisture through the atmosphere, and can see inside storms, including hurricanes.

statements.text: Radar is an active instrument: it sends out pulses of energy and measures what is reflected back.
How far radar reaches into a forest depends on its wavelength: a C-band signal only gets into the top layers of the canopy.

conditions.label: Works at night
conditions.text: Radar makes its own pulses, so it images night or day.

conditions.label: Sees through cloud
conditions.text: Radar imaging works regardless of weather conditions.

uses.text: The Copernicus Emergency Management Service maps floods worldwide from Sentinel-1, in under 8 hours, whatever the cloud or light.
The European Ground Motion Service measures ground movement across Europe to the millimetre, from Sentinel-1 radar interferometry.

statements.text: Altimeters are active instruments: they send pulses down to the surface and use the reflections to measure its height.
Satellite altimeters measure sea surface height over the oceans and coasts.

uses.text: Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich is the reference mission for the Copernicus Marine Service, which combines every altimeter flying to monitor sea level.
SWOT measures rivers wider than 100 m and lakes of 15 acres or more.

statements.text: Sentinel-5P measures the atmosphere for air quality, ozone and UV radiation, and climate monitoring and forecasting.

conditions.label: Needs sunlight
conditions.text: These spectrometers read sunlight, so their maps have gaps where there is no sunlight or the cloud is too thick.

uses.text: The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service has fed TROPOMI's nitrogen dioxide into its forecasts since October 2021.
The Support to Aviation Control Service sends volcanic sulphur dioxide and ash alerts to aviation, using TROPOMI and other instruments.

statements.text: Laser altimeters are active instruments: they send out pulses of light and measure what is reflected back.
GEDI uses laser ranging to measure Earth's forests and topography in high resolution.

conditions.label: Blocked by cloud
conditions.text: Clouds and particles in the air can skew a laser altimeter's ground data.

statements.text: Spectral resolution is an instrument's ability to tell finer wavelengths apart, with more and narrower bands.
EMIT uses this to map the minerals on Earth's surface in the regions that produce dust.
ABI detects visible and infrared light in 16 spectral bands.
It can capture a full-disk image every 10 minutes, the US mainland every five minutes, and smaller areas every 30 to 60 seconds.
Band 2 sees red visible light at 0.64 µm, and band 13, the clean longwave window, sees infrared at 10.3 µm.

specs.text: ABI: band 2 at 0.5 km, and a full-disk image every 10 minutes.

statements.text: AHI has 16 bands and scans the full disk every 10 minutes.

specs.text: AHI: band 3 at 0.5 km, and a full-disk scan every 10 minutes.

statements.text: VIIRS measures 22 spectral bands from 0.402 to 12.49 µm, with pixels of 375 m and 750 m.
Its false-colour view combines shortwave infrared (band M11, 2.23–2.28 µm), near infrared (I2, 0.85–0.88 µm) and red light (I1, 0.6–0.68 µm).
It flies on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21.

specs.text: VIIRS: 375 m pixels, and images of the whole Earth twice a day.

statements.text: MODIS sees every point on Earth every 1 to 2 days, in 36 spectral bands from 0.4 to 14.4 µm.
Its daily land surface temperature product has pixels 1 km across.

specs.text: MODIS: 250 m pixels, and global coverage every 1 to 2 days.

statements.text: MSI samples 13 spectral bands, from visible and near infrared to shortwave infrared: four at 10 m, six at 20 m and three at 60 m.
Its images serve land management, agriculture, forestry, disaster control and humanitarian relief.

specs.text: MSI: 10 m pixels; two Sentinel-2 satellites revisit every 5 days. Band edges are worked out from Copernicus's centre and width.

statements.text: OLI captures Earth's surface in visible, near infrared and shortwave infrared light.

specs.text: OLI: 30 m pixels; Landsat 8 and 9 together cover the land every 8 days.

statements.text: TIRS measures two thermal infrared bands, 10.6–11.19 µm and 11.50–12.51 µm, with 100 m pixels.
It works at 5.405 GHz, a wavelength of about 5.55 cm, and images Earth day and night, regardless of the weather.
Its images are used to identify sea ice, detect oil spills and measure ground movement from earthquakes, volcanoes and landslides.

specs.text: Sentinel-1: 5 m by 20 m pixels in its main mode, and a 6-day repeat with two satellites.

statements.text: TROPOMI looks across a swath about 2,600 km wide.
Its products include nitrogen dioxide and methane.

specs.text: TROPOMI: 3.5 by 5.5 km pixels since August 2019, and daily coverage.

statements.text: SMAP launched with a radar and a radiometer. The radar stopped in early 2015 when its power supply failed, and the radiometer carries on.

specs.text: SMAP radiometer: 1.41 GHz, a 38 by 49 km footprint, and the whole Earth every 2 to 3 days.

statements.text: OLCI measures the colour of the ocean and land in 21 bands, with 300 m pixels.

specs.text: OLCI: 300 m pixels, and under 1.9 days between looks with two satellites.

instruments.name: Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR)

statements.text: SLSTR measures global sea surface temperature to better than 0.3 K.
Sentinel-3 also makes fire monitoring products, such as fire radiated power and burned area.

specs.text: SLSTR: 500 m in visible light, 1 km in thermal infrared, and 0.9 days between looks with two satellites.

statements.text: SRAL is a dual-frequency Ku- and C-band radar altimeter that measures sea surface height for oceans and coasts.
SWOT is making the first global survey of Earth's surface water and measuring how water bodies change over time.
Its 120 km wide swath gives overlapping measurements over most of the globe, revisiting on average every 11 days.

specs.text: SWOT: rivers as narrow as 100 m, on a 21-day cycle.

statements.text: ECOSTRESS makes high-resolution images of the temperature of Earth's surface, to learn how much water plants use and when they become stressed.
GEDI measures Earth's forests and topography with high-resolution laser ranging from the ISS.

instruments.name: Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT)

statements.text: EMIT is an imaging spectrometer that maps the composition of minerals on Earth's surface where dust comes from.
Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich, launched in November 2020, is the latest in the series of satellites that have measured global sea level since 1993.
NASA's maps of the 2025 Arctic sea ice minimum were made from AMSR2 on JAXA's GCOM-W1 satellite.
OMI on NASA's Aura satellite measures nitrogen dioxide, as TROPOMI does.
The ISS is an orbiting laboratory. 2 November 2025 marked 25 years of continuous human presence aboard it.
Earth-observing instruments mounted on the station include ECOSTRESS, GEDI and EMIT.
The first MODIS was launched on Terra in December 1999.
Since 2020, Terra has been drifting to an earlier equator crossing time, with no manoeuvres planned to hold it.
NASA expects Terra and Aqua, which carry MODIS, to begin shutting down in late 2026 or early 2027.
The second MODIS was launched on Aqua in May 2002.

Himawari-9 took over the main operational role on 13 December 2022, about 35,800 km above the equator near 140.7°E.

lessons.title: Light or heat?
lessons.summary: Compare GOES East's visible and infrared views, and see why one keeps working at night.

text.text: GOES-19 is NOAA's GOES East satellite. Its imager, ABI, detects visible and infrared light in 16 spectral bands.
This is band 2: red visible light at 0.64 µm. Visible light is the part of the spectrum our eyes can see, so this is much how the Americas would look to us.

question.prompt: Find the night side of the disk, if there is one right now. What will an infrared band show there?
choices: Nothing, just like the visible band

explain.text: NOAA likens its infrared channels to night-vision goggles, because they see by day and by night.

text.text: This is band 13, the clean longwave window, at 10.3 µm. Warm surfaces give off infrared radiation, so this band senses heat rather than reflected light.

steps.hint: If the whole disk is in daylight right now, the two views look alike. Come back in a few hours to see the night side.

text.text: Forecasters use cloud-top temperatures from infrared as predictors of rainfall intensity and flash flooding.
ABI can capture this whole disk every 10 minutes, so the views you see are close to live.

steps.hint: Switch between the two views to compare them.

lessons.title: Colours you can't see
lessons.summary: Use NOAA-20's shortwave and near infrared to find plants, burn scars and ice.

text.text: NOAA-20 carries VIIRS, which measures 22 spectral bands from 0.402 to 12.49 µm. This is yesterday's true-colour view of the whole Earth from VIIRS.

question.prompt: In a view that uses near-infrared light, how will forests and grassland look next to bare desert?

explain.text: Plants reflect near-infrared light very strongly, so vegetated land stands out.

text.text: This view combines shortwave infrared (band M11, 2.23–2.28 µm), near infrared (I2, 0.85–0.88 µm) and red light (I1, 0.6–0.68 µm).
Plants reflect near infrared very strongly, so vegetated land shows bright green in this view.

steps.hint: Look at Africa and compare the land south of the Sahara with the desert.

question.prompt: Antarctica is covered in ice. Ice reflects visible light but absorbs infrared. Which colour will it be?

explain.text: In a shortwave infrared, near infrared and green combination, snow and ice look bright blue, water black, and newly burned land red.

text.text: Newly burned land reflects strongly in shortwave infrared, which makes this kind of view valuable for mapping fire damage.

steps.hint: Between April and September, Antarctica is in polar night and shows black. Turn the globe to Greenland instead.

lessons.title: The orbit decides the data
lessons.summary: Why GOES sees one side of Earth every 10 minutes, while Terra sees all of it every day or two.

text.text: A geostationary satellite circles once in the time Earth takes to turn, above the equator, so it watches the same side of Earth all the time.
That is why GOES-19 can capture this disk every 10 minutes. It never sees the far side of the planet.

question.prompt: Terra flies low over the poles instead. How often can its MODIS camera see any one place?

explain.text: MODIS sees every point on Earth every 1 to 2 days, in 36 spectral bands.

text.text: Satellites in a polar orbit pass roughly over Earth's poles at low altitude, while Earth turns beneath them, so they see a different strip on every orbit.
This daily land temperature map is built from those MODIS strips. Clouds leave gaps, because most passive sensors cannot see through dense cloud.
It is difficult to combine every desirable feature in one instrument: a sharper view needs a narrower swath, which means more time between observations.

steps.hint: Open the Orbit tab to see why each satellite flies where it does.

lessons.title: The night Puerto Rico went dark
lessons.summary: Suomi NPP's night-time camera before and after Hurricane Maria.

text.text: This is Puerto Rico on a night in July 2017, seen by the Day/Night Band of VIIRS on Suomi NPP, which detects light from green to near-infrared wavelengths.

question.prompt: Hurricane Maria crossed the island on 20 September. What will the same view show a week later?

explain.text: Maria knocked down 80 percent of Puerto Rico's utility poles and all transmission lines, and essentially all of the island's 3.4 million residents lost power.

text.text: Maria's centre crossed the southeast coast near Yabucoa at about 10:15 UTC on 20 September 2017.
NASA's own comparison, using the nights of 27 and 28 September, showed outages around San Juan, including hospitals and transport.
By the end of January 2018, electricity had been restored to about 65 percent of the island.

lessons.title: Los Angeles fires, January 2025
lessons.summary: Smoke in visible light, burning land in shortwave infrared, and fire detections from VIIRS.

text.text: The Palisades Fire started on the morning of 7 January 2025. The Eaton Fire broke out shortly afterwards and grew to more than 200 acres within an hour.

steps.hint: This is Terra's true-colour view on 8 January. Look for smoke blowing out over the ocean.

question.prompt: Which kind of light picks out the hottest part of a fire?

explain.text: A shortwave infrared band at 3.9 µm is sensitive to the hottest part of a fire, so GOES often detects fires before they are spotted on the ground.

text.text: Newly burned land reflects strongly in shortwave infrared, which makes it valuable for mapping fire damage.

steps.hint: Switch between the two views of the same day.

text.text: VIIRS detects smaller, lower-temperature fires because its pixels are 375 m across. Each dot is a fire detection.
GOES West sent forecasters one-minute data of the fires.
By 21 January, the Palisades Fire had burned 23,713 acres and the Eaton Fire 14,021 acres, and more than 12,000 structures had been destroyed.

lessons.title: Mapping a flood through the clouds
lessons.summary: Sentinel-1's radar maps Hurricane Helene's storm surge when cloud blocks other satellites.

text.text: On 26 September 2024, Hurricane Helene made landfall in the Big Bend area of Florida's Gulf Coast as a Category 4 storm, with 15 feet of storm surge.
This is a map of surface water on 14 September, before the storm, made from Sentinel-1 radar by NASA JPL's OPERA project.

question.prompt: Clouds covered the coast during the storm. Which data could still map the flooding?
choices: Visible images from Landsat and Sentinel-2

explain.text: Radar water maps can see water and the ground day or night and through cloud. Optical maps from Landsat and Sentinel-2 were limited by cloud during Helene.

text.text: NASA mapped the storm surge by comparing a water map from 14 September, before the storm, with one from 26 September, after it.

steps.hint: Switch between the two dates and look along the coast.

lessons.title: Cleaner air during the 2020 lockdowns
lessons.summary: Satellites measured nitrogen dioxide falling over China and Europe in early 2020.

text.text: NASA compared nitrogen dioxide over China from 1–20 January 2020, before the quarantine, with 10–25 February, during it, using TROPOMI.
This map is one day from OMI on NASA's Aura satellite, which makes similar measurements.

question.prompt: OMI compared early 2020 with the 2005–2019 average for the same time of year. How much lower was nitrogen dioxide in eastern and central China?

explain.text: Nitrogen dioxide in eastern and central China was 10 to 30 percent lower, and researchers judged the drop to be more than a holiday or weather effect.

text.text: Nitrogen dioxide changes with the weather from day to day, so ESA's comparisons average a month, with an uncertainty of 15 percent.

steps.hint: Single days have gaps where it was cloudy, so compare the overall pattern.

chart.title: Drop in nitrogen dioxide, 13 March to 13 April 2020, against March–April 2019

source.text: ESA's Sentinel-5P maps show decreases of around 45 percent in Madrid, Milan and Rome, and 54 percent in Paris.

text.text: In Europe, TROPOMI on Sentinel-5P showed nitrogen dioxide from 13 March to 13 April 2020 well below the March–April averages of 2019.

lessons.title: Lake Mead shrinks
lessons.summary: Two July days, 22 years apart, seen from orbit.

text.text: NASA compared natural-colour Landsat images of Lake Mead from 6 July 2000 and 3 July 2022. This is the same day in 2000, seen by MODIS on Terra.

question.prompt: By July 2022, how full was Lake Mead?

explain.text: On 18 July 2022 the water at Hoover Dam stood at 1,041.30 feet (317.4 m) above sea level, the lowest since 1937, and the lake was 27 percent full.

text.text: Lake Mead supplies water to millions of people across seven states, tribal lands and northern Mexico.
Closer, from Landsat. NASA describes the light-coloured fringes along the shore as mineralised areas of the lakeshore.

lessons.title: Three decades of rising seas
lessons.summary: Five satellites in a row have measured the height of the sea since 1993.

chart.title: Global mean sea level from satellite altimeters

text.text: Since satellites began measuring sea surface height in 1993 with TOPEX/Poseidon, global average sea level rose 9.1 cm (3.6 inches) through 2022.
This chart is NOAA's record from TOPEX/Poseidon, the Jason satellites and Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich.

question.prompt: Has the rise sped up since 1993, or stayed steady?

explain.text: NASA's record from five satellites shows the rate of rise has more than doubled in three decades. In 2024 it was 0.59 cm a year, against an expected 0.43 cm.

text.text: In 2024, two-thirds of the rise came from seawater expanding as it warmed, the reverse of recent years.
Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich, launched in November 2020, is the latest satellite in this record.

steps.hint: Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich is now on the globe. Open Orbit to see why it flies where it does.

lessons.title: Arctic sea ice at its summer low
lessons.summary: Microwave radiometers have measured Arctic sea ice since 1979.

text.text: Passive microwave satellites have tracked Arctic sea ice continuously since 1979.
This is the ice on 16 September 2012, measured by AMSR2 on GCOM-W1. 2012 has the lowest extent on record.

question.prompt: Between 1979 and 2012, how much did the area of the summer minimum shrink?

explain.text: NASA's satellite measurements of the minimum each year from 1979 to 2012 show the area shrinking by half.

text.text: The 2025 minimum, probably reached on 10 September, measured 4.60 million square kilometres.
It tied 2008 for the 10th lowest on record.

steps.hint: The 2025 picture is from 1 September, the last day this layer has.

chart.title: Arctic sea ice extent each September

text.text: NSIDC's Sea Ice Index gives the average Arctic extent for each September since 1979.

regions_sources.text: Visible light is 0.4 to 0.7 µm, and microwaves 1 mm to 1 m.
NASA puts near infrared at 0.7 to 1.1 µm and shortwave infrared at 1.1 to 3 µm; WMO puts the split at 1.3 µm.
Mid-wave infrared, 3 to 5 µm, holds an atmospheric window for surface temperature and clouds.
Earth scientists call 8 to 15 µm thermal infrared.
Radar C band is 4 to 8 GHz, 3.8 to 7.5 cm, and L band 1 to 2 GHz, 15 to 30 cm.
